summary: Describes a simple method for encoding telephone numbers of fax machines in the local part of email addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: This document says how to write the phone number of a fax machine in an email address, so that a mail gateway knows which number to dial and which sub-address to use when it sends the fax on.

questions: send fax by email address format
what is a fax email address
what is t33s in a fax address
how do i write a fax number as an email address
subtitle: How to write a fax machine's telephone number as the local part of an ordinary email address.

tldr.problem: Fax gateways had to invent their own way of writing a fax number in an email address, so a sender could not know which form a given gateway would accept.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the fax service-selector as FAX, the fax number as an international global phone number after an equals sign, and one optional extension element, T33S, for the numeric sub-addresses that the T.33 fax routing recommendation uses.
tldr.outcome: There is one agreed way to write a fax address, with the sub-address carried in a registered extension element. The document obsoletes RFC 2304 and updates RFC 2846.

facts.label: Global phone form
facts.value: A plus sign followed by digits

facts.label: Permitted separators
facts.value: Hyphen and dot, ignored by implementations

facts.label: Multiple sub-addresses
facts.value: Each one needs its own fax-email address

today: RFC 3192 is a Draft Standard from October 2001 that obsoletes RFC 2304 and updates RFC 2846, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
As with all Internet mail addresses, the left-hand side, the local part, of an address generated according to this specification is not to be interpreted except by the MTA that is named on the right-hand side, the domain.

Since the very first email to fax gateway objects appeared, implementors have used a number of different methods to specify a fax address as an email address. Several objectives for these methods have been identified: to enable an email user to send and receive faxes from their email interface, and to allow some kind of fax over email service transport, possibly reducing the cost of GSTN long distance transmissions, while using the existing email infrastructure.

The memo describes the minimal addressing method and the standard extensions needed to encode fax addresses into email addresses, as required by the companion GSTN address specification. The opposite problem, letting a traditional numeric-only fax device user reach the email transport service, is not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax-to-mail gateways each chose their own format for the number, so a sender could not be sure what a gateway would accept. This document fixes one format for fax, built on the general GSTN address rules.

sections.title: The Minimal Fax Address
sections.content:
The minimal fax address within email has been defined for consistency with the GSTN minimal address specification, and it contains two elements: the fax-mbox and an optional extension element. The GSTN minimal address specification requires a unique service-selector for each specific application, and the service-selector defined for the fax service is simply the string FAX.

In the syntax for the fax address an extension element has been defined to support the T.30 and T.33 sub-addresses. The use of this element is optional, but compliant implementations must be able to support and correctly interpret it when it is present. Its definition is a slash, the T33S separator, an equals sign and the sub-address, where the separator is the string T33S and the sub-address is one or more digits. The minimal specification of a fax address in an email address is therefore a fax-mbox with an optional T33S sub-address, where the fax-mbox is the string FAX, an equals sign and a global phone number.

Two notes apply to the sub-address. For the case of a single sub-address, only numbers are allowed, which is consistent with T.30, T.33 and this document; while T.30 and T.33 use the space character to pad their field, padding is not necessary in the sub-address field defined here. For the case of multiple sub-addresses, T.33 specifies that the hash character be used, but only digits are permitted in the sub-address field defined by this document, and Section 4.1 describes how to specify more than one sub-address per fax-mbox.
sections.plainLanguage: The fax address is the word FAX, an equals sign and the number. If the fax has a sub-address, as used by the T.33 routing recommendation, it follows as a slash and T33S and then digits only.

sections.title: The global-phone Element
sections.content:
The minimal supported syntax for global-phone, as described in the GSTN minimal address specification, is a plus sign followed by one or more digits or written separators, where a written separator is a hyphen or a dot. The companion GSTN document covers the other important considerations about the global-phone element, including that other dialing schemes must not use the leading plus sign, that the plus sign is strictly reserved for the standard global-phone syntax, and that any written separators must be ignored by conformant implementations.

The examples given for the minimal fax address are FAX=+3940226338, FAX=+12027653000/T33S=1387 and FAX=+33-1-88335215. The examples are shown for illustration purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The number is written in international form, with a plus sign and then digits. Hyphens and dots may be inserted and must be ignored on receipt.

sections.title: The mta-I-fax Part of the Address
sections.content:
An I-fax device has, among its characteristics, a unique Internet domain name that identifies it on the Internet. Within Internet mail this is the right-hand side of the address, the part on the right of the at sign, and this document calls it the mta-I-fax, which is simply a domain.

For domain strings used in SMTP transmissions the string must conform to the requirements of the standards for domains, and for domain strings used in message content headers it must conform to the requirements of the relevant standards. The use of domain names or domain literals is permitted in addresses in both the SMTP envelope and the message header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The right-hand side is the ordinary domain of the fax device or of the gateway that will place the call, with the same rules as any other email address.

sections.title: The fax-email Structure
sections.content:
The complete structure used to transfer a minimal fax address over the Internet email transport system is called the fax-email. It is an email address conforming to the addr-spec syntax, with structure refinements that allow the fax number to be identified: optionally a quote character, optionally a slash, the fax-address, optionally a slash, optionally a quote character, then the at sign and the mta-I-fax.

Implementors' note: the optional slash characters can result from translations from other transport gateways, such as some X.400 gateways, which have included the slash as an optional element. Implementations must accept the optional slashes but should not generate them, and gateways are allowed to strip them off when converting to Internet mail addressing. The relevant standards define exactly when the optional quote characters surrounding the entire local part must be added.

There are some instances in GSTN applications where multiple sub-addresses are used, and T.33 sub-addresses in the fax service are one of these cases. In email practice a separate and unique email address is always used for each recipient, so if multiple T.33 sub-addresses are present, the use of multiple fax-email elements is required. Implementors' note: the user agent may accept multiple sub-address elements for the same global-phone, but it must generate multiple fax-mbox elements when submitting the message to the MTA.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole thing is an ordinary email address whose local part holds the fax number. Each fax sub-address needs its own email address, because one address must mean one recipient.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies a means by which fax addresses can be encoded into email addresses. Since email routing is determined by DNS data, a successful attack on DNS could disseminate tampered information, which causes email messages to be diverted via some MTA or gateway where the security of the software has been compromised.

There are several means by which an attacker might be able to deliver incorrect mail routing information to a client: compromise of a DNS server, generating a counterfeit response to a client's DNS query, and returning incorrect additional information in response to an unrelated query. Clients should ensure that mail routing is based only on authoritative answers. Once DNS security mechanisms become more widely deployed, clients should employ those mechanisms to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail goes where DNS says it goes, so an attacker who can answer DNS queries can divert a fax to a machine they control. Clients should trust only authoritative answers, and use DNS security once it is widely deployed.

sections.title: The Two IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The IANA registration forms for the FAX service-selector and the T33S extension element are defined in the document, and they update the previous registration forms defined in the GSTN address element extensions specification.

The FAX service-selector registration gives the name FAX and describes its use as specifying that the GSTN address refers either to an Internet fax device or to an onramp or offramp fax gateway, with a complete description in RFC 3192 and RFC 3191. The T33S registration gives the keyword name T33S, the ABNF definition of the value as one or more digits, and describes it as the numeric-only optional fax sub-address element described in the ITU T.33 recommendation on facsimile routing using the sub-address, with a further detailed description in RFC 3192. The use of T33S is restricted to the FAX service-selector, as it has no meaning outside the fax service. Both forms carry the security considerations of this document and the contact information of the author.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are registered with IANA: FAX for the service, and T33S for the sub-address. T33S is restricted to fax addresses and means nothing anywhere else.

sections.title: Changes since RFC 2304
sections.content: There are no major or technical changes from the RFC 2304 specification, and the section records where updates and clarifications were introduced. Considering the case that telephony systems no longer conform to the single or few Public Operator paradigm, the old definition PSTN, Public Switched Telephone Network, was changed into the more adequate GSTN, Global Switched Telephone Network, although the ABNF variable names were not changed for consistency with the previous specification. Section 7, the IANA considerations, and the IANA registration forms for the FAX service-selector and for the T33S extension element were added. The changes also included the addition of the fax-email syntax and examples, the clarification of the multiple sub-addresses rule, and the update of the references list.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules did not change. The earlier version was tidied up: the old acronym for the telephone network was replaced, the registration forms were added, and the examples and the rule for several sub-addresses were made explicit.

viz.caption: What the fax format is for

items.title: Send and receive faxes from mail
items.text: One of the objectives is to let an email user send and receive faxes from their email interface.

items.title: Use the existing mail network
items.text: Another objective is a fax over email service that reuses the existing email infrastructure, possibly reducing the cost of long distance telephone calls.

items.title: The I-fax device
items.text: A device with a unique Internet domain name that identifies it on the Internet; that domain is the right-hand side of the address.

items.title: Not the other direction
items.text: The opposite problem, letting a traditional numeric-only fax device reach the email service, is not discussed.

data.title: Minimal fax address
data.code:
service-selector = "FAX"

qualif-type1 = "/" t33-sep "=" sub-addr

t33-sep = "T33S"

sub-addr = 1*( DIGIT )

fax-address = fax-mbox [ "/T33S=" sub-addr ]

fax-mbox = "FAX=" global-phone

viz.caption: The number syntax and the examples from the RFC

data.title: global-phone
data.code:
global-phone = "+" 1*( DIGIT / written-sep )

written-sep = ( "-" / "." )

Examples of a minimal fax-address:

FAX=+3940226338
FAX=+12027653000/T33S=1387
FAX=+33-1-88335215

viz.caption: The whole address and the examples from the RFC

data.title: fax-email
data.code:
fax-email = ["""] ["/"] fax-address ["/"] ["""] "@" mta-I-fax

Examples of minimal fax-email addresses:

FAX=+3940226338@faxworld.org

FAX=+12027653000/T33S=1387@faxworld.org

/FAX=+33-1-88335215/@faxworld.org

viz.caption: The two names registered with IANA

items.title: FAX, the service-selector
items.text: Says that the address refers either to an Internet fax device or to a gateway that sends or receives faxes.

items.title: T33S, the extension element
items.text: Carries the numeric-only optional fax sub-address described in the ITU T.33 recommendation on facsimile routing using the sub-address.

items.title: Restricted to fax
items.text: The use of T33S is restricted to the FAX service-selector, because it has no meaning outside the fax service.

viz.caption: How mail routing can be tampered with

items.title: Compromise of a DNS server
items.text: An attacker who controls a name server can send the wrong routing information.

items.title: A counterfeit answer
items.text: An attacker can reply to the client's own DNS query with a false answer.

items.title: Incorrect additional information
items.text: An unrelated query can carry back additional records that a client then uses.

items.title: What clients should do
items.text: Base mail routing only on authoritative answers, and use DNS security mechanisms to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
